chunks: "Because capacitors in parallel only add up like ideal capacitors at low frequency.
A real capacitor has series inductance, so above its self-resonant frequency it's an inductor, and a bigger capacitor in a bigger package has a lower self-resonance, not a higher one.
A single 100 microfarad part might stop being capacitive at a few hundred kilohertz, and above that its impedance climbs at 2 pi f times its ESL.
At the frequencies where fast digital current lives, tens to hundreds of megahertz, it's basically a small inductor. Using many smaller capacitors fixes that in two ways.
Electrically, N capacitors in parallel divide the ESL and the mounting inductance by N, so ten 10 microfarad capacitors have a tenth of the inductance of one, with the same total capacitance.
Physically, the current has to be supplied near every power pin, and one capacitor can only be near one place; a chip with dozens of supply pins needs charge close to each.
And using different values covers different bands: big ones for lower frequencies, small ones with the highest self-resonance for the top end.
The catch is that mixing values makes anti-resonance peaks between them, so I check the combined impedance against a target and damp the peaks with ESR if needed."
